heading: Choices and trade-offs
body:
For Go, a release build tries TinyGo first. When TinyGo is not installed, or it cannot compile your services (some packages, reflection or `//go:linkname` are limited in TinyGo), the build compiles them again with the standard Go compiler and prints why. It never fails only because TinyGo failed. Each compiler ships its own `wasm_exec.js`, and Tachyon publishes the one that matches the module. A call from the page still waits for a `time.Sleep` inside it, as with the standard compiler. TinyGo builds with the Boehm garbage collector (`-gc=boehm`). Each call from the page runs in a new goroutine with its own 64 KB stack, and TinyGo's default collector swept the whole heap every few calls, so one call in four or five paused for 3 to 5 ms. With Boehm the slowest 5% of calls take under 1 ms. It costs about 47 KiB raw and 14 KiB with Brotli (ADR 0081). To choose the compiler yourself, set `tac.go.compiler` in `client/manifest.json`: `"tinygo"` uses TinyGo in every build, also in `ty preview`, with no fallback; `"go"` never uses TinyGo. Use `"tinygo"` while you develop when you want to find TinyGo limits before a release.

For C# and F#, the default is the trimmed .NET interpreter. It downloads the least and runs services that hold state and logic well. When a service does heavy computing (for example image or number work in a loop), set `tac.dotnet.aot` to `true` in `client/manifest.json`. The release build then compiles the services ahead of time (AOT). They run faster, but the download is larger and the build takes minutes. Tachyon does not guess which services need AOT; the release line reminds you of the setting.

For Dart, the release setting `-O4` assumes that the program has no type errors. Development builds keep `-O2`, which checks types while the service runs, so a type error shows up in `ty preview` first.

Most of a Swift module is the Swift standard library and its runtime, so even a small Swift service is about 3.5 MiB (about 980 KiB as sent with Brotli). Other settings do not help: after Binaryen, linker flags such as `--strip-all` save nothing, and leaving out reflection metadata saves 2 KB but changes what `String(describing:)` prints. Embedded Swift would make a small counter about 33 KB (12 KB with Brotli), but it has no `Codable`, no `Any` values, no `as?` casts and no `throws` without an error type, and Swift services use all of them. So Tachyon keeps the full standard library (ADR 0082). When the download matters most, write the service in Rust or Dart.

The table shows the WebAssembly that the page downloads for one small service (the tally from the WebAssembly services example), before and after this change, as a raw file and as sent with Brotli (see Compressed files). Route size budgets measure these smaller files.

| Language | Before, raw | After, raw | Before, Brotli | After, Brotli | Smaller (Brotli) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rust | 142.1 KiB | 109.2 KiB | 56.7 KiB | 48.6 KiB | 14% |
| Go | 3.09 MiB | 356.5 KiB | 678.5 KiB | 112.7 KiB | 83% |
| C# | 2.87 MiB | 2.83 MiB | 943.0 KiB | 938.7 KiB | under 1% |
| Dart | 47.0 KiB | 45.6 KiB | 16.8 KiB | 16.5 KiB | 2% |
| Kotlin | 293 KB | 101 KB | | | (ADR 0078) |
| Swift | 3.30 MiB | 3.23 MiB | | 897.7 KiB | (ADR 0082) |
| Java | 134.7 KiB | 70.8 KiB | 46.5 KiB | 29.8 KiB | 36% |

Go gains the most, because TinyGo leaves out most of the Go runtime. On this website, a release build now publishes 8.7 MB instead of 11.7 MB, and sends 2.25 MB instead of 2.86 MB with Brotli; its Go module went from 684 KiB to 101 KiB as sent. The .NET browser runtime was already trimmed, so C# gains little; most of its download is the runtime itself, which the service worker caches once.
